lessons.title: Lesson 1: Matching the tool to the job
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Sort common athlete jobs into the right type of tool.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of common athlete or coach jobs, you will identify which type of tool fits each job: an AI assistant, a design tool, a spreadsheet or a tracker, getting at least 4 of 5 jobs right.
There are hundreds of AI apps, but most fit into a few types. AI assistants (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini) write, explain and plan. Design tools (like Canva) make graphics and short videos. Spreadsheets (Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel) keep and chart your numbers. Fitness trackers and team video apps collect data from your body or your games.
Start with the job, not the app. "I need a weekly plan" points to an assistant. "I need a game-day post" points to a design tool. "I want to see if my sprint time is improving" points to a spreadsheet.
Free versions are usually enough to start. Learn one tool of each type well before adding more.
Words to know:
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with to write, explain or plan.
- Spreadsheet: a grid of rows and columns for keeping and charting numbers.
Try it now: List five jobs you do as an athlete or coach each week (for example plan workouts, post on social media, track a stat). Next to each, write which tool type fits.
You can now match an athlete job to the right type of AI tool.

check.q: Which type of tool keeps your numbers and turns them into a chart?
check.why: Spreadsheets like Google Sheets and Excel keep and chart numbers.

check.q: A teammate wants to try five new apps this week. What would you suggest?
options: Pay for the most expensive one
Start with the job, then learn one free tool of that type well
check.why: The lesson says start with the job and learn one tool of each type well first.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: An AI assistant as your planner
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to turn your schedule into a clear weekly plan.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant and your real schedule, you will create a weekly plan in a table and improve it with follow-up requests, with every fixed time included and coach-set training left unchanged.
An AI assistant is great at turning a messy list into a plan. Give it your practices, games, classes and work shifts, and ask for a weekly plan in a table.
Be specific: "I'm a college volleyball player. Practice is 2-5 pm Monday to Friday, games Saturday. Classes are 9-12. Make a weekly table with study blocks, meals and sleep times." Then improve it with follow-ups like "Add 30 minutes for film on Wednesday."
The assistant plans; your coach sets the training. Do not ask it to change workouts your coach wrote, and check anything about health or rest with your athletic trainer.
Step by step:
- List your fixed times: practices, games, classes, work.
- Ask for a weekly plan in a table.
- Ask for one change at a time.
- Copy the final plan into your calendar or notes.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second request that changes or builds on the answer.
Try it now: Type your real fixed times for next week into an AI assistant and ask for a weekly plan in a table. Ask for one improvement.
You can now turn your schedule into a weekly plan with an AI assistant.

check.q: What makes a planning request to an AI assistant work well?
options: Being specific about your sport and fixed times
Asking it to rewrite your coach's workouts
check.why: Specific details about your schedule give a plan that fits your real week.

check.q: Your plan needs 30 minutes of film on Wednesday. What do you do?
options: Start a new chat from scratch
Ask your athletic trainer to write it
Ask the assistant for that one change as a follow-up
check.why: Follow-ups that ask for one change at a time improve the plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making a game-day graphic with Canva
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple game-day graphic using a free design template.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free Canva template, you will create a game-day graphic that shows who, when and where with one strong photo, readable on a phone in two seconds and using only photos and logos you have permission to use.
Canva is a free design tool on the web and as an app. It has ready-made templates for social posts, flyers and stories, and it includes AI features that can suggest text or images.
A clean game-day graphic has four things: who is playing, when, where, and one strong photo. Use your team colors, big readable text, and nothing more.
Use only photos you took or have permission to use. Many schools have rules about using school logos and names, so ask your athletic department before posting a graphic with official logos.
Step by step:
- Open Canva and search templates for "game day".
- Pick a template sized for the platform you use.
- Change the text: opponent, date, time, place.
- Swap in your own photo and team colors.
- Download it and check it on your phone before posting.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you change to make your own.
- Permission: a yes from the owner to use their photo, logo or name.
Try it now: Make a game-day graphic in Canva for your next game or practice. Check it on your phone: can you read the time and place in two seconds?
You can now make a clean game-day graphic from a template and use photos and logos the right way.

options: A free design tool with templates for posts and flyers
check.why: Canva is a free design tool on the web and as an app with ready-made templates.

check.q: You finished your graphic. What should you do before posting it?
options: Download it and check it on your phone
Swap in a photo you found online
check.why: Checking on a phone shows whether the time and place can be read quickly.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Tracking, judging and building your kit

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Tracking one stat in Google Sheets
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a sheet that tracks one stat and shows it as a chart.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets, you will set up a sheet that tracks one stat by date and chart the trend, with at least three sessions entered, the stat measured the same way each time, and the sheet shared only with people you choose.
Pick one stat that matters to you and that you can measure the same way each time: free-throw makes out of 20, 40-yard time, mile time, or serve accuracy.
In Google Sheets, make two columns: Date and your stat. Add a row after each session. When you have a few rows, select both columns and insert a chart to see the trend.
You can ask an AI assistant to explain spreadsheet steps or a formula, like how to get your average. Keep the sheet private unless you choose to share it with your coach.
Step by step:
- Open Google Sheets and start a blank sheet.
- Type "Date" in A1 and your stat in B1.
- Add one row after each session.
- Select both columns and insert a chart.
- Share it only with your coach if you want feedback.
Words to know:
- Trend: the direction your numbers move over time: up, down or flat.
- Formula: a short instruction in a cell that does math, like an average.
Try it now: Set up a Google Sheet for one stat. Enter at least three past sessions (or practice numbers) and insert a chart.
You can now track one stat in a spreadsheet and chart it to see your trend.

check.q: What two columns does your stat sheet start with?
check.why: Date in column A and the stat in column B let you see the trend over time.

check.q: You want feedback on your stat sheet. What do you do?
options: Share it only with your coach
Send it to the other team
Print it for the locker room wall
check.why: Keep the sheet private and share it only with people you choose, like your coach.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The five-question app check
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Judge a new sports or AI app before you give it data or money.
This lesson builds toward: Given a new sports or AI app, you will check its maker, data, cost, team fit and promises using the five-question app check, answering all five questions and writing a clear decision: use it, try it carefully, or skip it.
New apps promise to make you faster, get you recruited or grow your following. Before signing up, run a quick five-question check.
1. Who makes it, and is it in the official app store? 2. What data does it collect, and can you delete it? (Read the privacy policy summary.) 3. What does it cost after the free trial? 4. Does your coach or school already use something similar? 5. Does it promise results that sound too good, like guaranteed scholarships?
Body and health data, like heart rate, sleep and location, is private. Only share it with apps you trust, and turn off location sharing you do not need.
Step by step:
- Check who makes it and that it is in the official store.
- Read what data it collects and how to delete it.
- Find the price after any free trial.
- Ask your coach what the team already uses.
- Walk away from guaranteed results.
Words to know:
- Privacy policy: the app's explanation of what data it collects and what it does with it.
- Free trial: a short free period before the app starts charging.
Try it now: Pick one sports or AI app you have seen advertised. Answer the five questions about it in a note and decide: use it, try it carefully, or skip it.
You can now check a new app's maker, data, cost and promises before you sign up.

check.q: Which of these is one of the five app-check questions?
options: How many ads does it show?
What does it cost after the free trial?
Does it have a dark mode?
check.why: Price after the trial is question 3 of the five-question check.

check.q: A training app asks to share your location all the time, but it does not need it. What do you do?
options: Allow it so the app works faster
check.why: Location is private data, so turn off sharing you do not need.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Putting your toolkit together
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use all three tools together for one real week.
This lesson builds toward: For one real week, you will plan a weekly routine that uses your planner, design tool and stats sheet together, with each tool given a set day or moment and team data shared only with staff who need it.
Your toolkit works best as a weekly routine. Sunday: use your AI assistant to plan the week. Before a game: make the graphic. After each session: add your stat to the sheet.
Write a short list of your tools and what each one is for, so you are not trying new apps every week. Add a new tool only when you have a job your kit cannot do.
Coaches can use the same kit for a team: a weekly plan for the staff, one graphic per game, and a shared sheet for team stats. Share team sheets only with staff who need them.
Step by step:
- Write your tool list: planner, design, sheet.
- Sunday: plan the week with the assistant.
- Game week: make one graphic.
- After each session: add your stat.
- Review the chart with your coach every few weeks.
Words to know:
- Routine: steps you repeat at the same time each week.
- Toolkit: the small set of tools you use again and again.
Try it now: Final task: plan next week with an AI assistant, make one game-day graphic in Canva, set up a sheet that tracks one stat, and run the five-question check on one new app.
You can now use a small set of free AI tools together as a weekly routine.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Weekly plan The plan is missing fixed times, or it changes the coach's training. A weekly table with all fixed times, study, meals and sleep, improved with at least one follow-up. The plan is copied into a calendar and health or rest questions are noted for the athletic trainer. Game-day graphic Who, when or where is missing, it is hard to read on a phone, or it uses photos or logos without permission. Shows who, when, where and one strong photo, readable on a phone in two seconds, with permitted images only. Uses team colors, is sized for the right platform, and logo use was cleared with the athletic department. Stat sheet No dates, fewer than three sessions, or no chart. Date and stat columns, at least three sessions measured the same way, and a chart of the trend. Five sessions entered, an average added, and the sheet shared only with the coach for feedback. App check Some of the five questions are unanswered or there is no decision. All five questions answered and a clear decision: use it, try it carefully, or skip it. The decision gives reasons from the privacy policy and price, and unneeded data sharing is turned off. Toolkit routine No tool list, or no set time for each tool. A written tool list with a set day or moment for planning, graphics and stats. The routine includes a regular chart review with the coach and a rule for when to add a new tool. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: In the weekly routine, when do you add your stat to the sheet?
options: Only when you set a record
check.why: Adding the stat after each session keeps the trend complete.

check.q: You have a job your current toolkit cannot do. What do you do?
options: Try a new app every week anyway
Add one new tool for that job and run the app check
check.why: Add a new tool only when you have a job your kit cannot do, and check it first.
